headline: Cornell's faculty voted 75-50: no confidence.
summary: Cornell's Faculty Senate voted 75-50 on Friday that it has no confidence in the administration's ability to deal with sexual assault. A former student says she was raped at a fraternity house in 2024 and is suing the university and seven men. The vote removes nobody. The trustees' chair says the president is the right leader to fix it.

cover_question.q: Why vote if it can't fire anyone?

cover_answer: Pressure. The trustees heard it and kept the president.
table_question: If most of your team votes no confidence in you, do you stay?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: At a big college in New York, the teachers voted 75 to 50 that they don't trust the people in charge to keep students safe. Picture a class where most hands go up to say the rules aren't working. A grown-up student was hurt, and the grown-ups are arguing over who should have done more. You're safe, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: The hands going up carry the whole vote, and the hurt stays unnamed. This age takes one vivid detail for the whole event, so the detail is the hands.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the hands going up and nothing to picture about the hurt. Cantor's work says what frightens a small child is what it can see. Expect "who got hurt?" A grown-up student, and the grown-ups are sorting out who should have done more.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: A former Cornell student says she was raped at a fraternity party in 2024 and the university let her down. The school punished some of the men; professors wanted more. Friday they voted 75-50 that they don't trust the leaders to fix it. Like a class voting on the principal: a message, but the school board decides.
8-12.why: Report, punishment, vote, board: a chain with a referee at the end. At 11 they want to know if the rule gets applied; the board is that answer.
8-12.why_long: An eleven-year-old is working out whether adults apply the rules, so the script hands over the chain: a report, a punishment some professors said fell short, a vote, and a board that decides anyway. Expect "so the vote did nothing?" It did one thing: the trustees' chair said the campus is angry. Then she backed the president.

13-17.script: Should leaders lose their jobs over how they handled something they didn't do? Cornell's professors voted 75-50 that they don't trust the leaders on sexual assault; a former student says she was raped at a fraternity. Second: 50 voted no, some to wait for an outside review. Is waiting confidence?
13-17.why: Two true things: 75 said the leaders failed, 50 said no, or not yet. At 13 they can hold both, and are testing whether you will argue it straight.
13-17.why_long: A thirteen-year-old can hold two true things, so the script gives both: 75 professors said the leaders failed, and 50 said no, some because an outside review isn't done. The second question sits on the 50: the harder side is the practice. Expect "were the men punished?" Two expelled, two suspended, two wrote papers. All seven deny it.

5-7.q: Why don't they trust the grown-ups in charge?
5-7.a: A student was hurt. The teachers think the bosses did too little.

8-12.a: No. The trustees pick the president, and their chair says he stays.

8-12.q: Why are the professors so angry?
8-12.a: Some say he didn't act forcefully enough. He asked for more time.

13-17.q: Why vote if it can't fire anyone?
13-17.a: Pressure on the trustees. Their chair spoke of anger, and backed him.
Two expelled, two suspended, two wrote papers. All seven deny it.
